## Key takeaways
- Meta rebuilt three systems. [Andromeda](#andromeda) picks which ads a person could see, [GEM](#gem) learns what each shopper wants, and [GenRecs](#genrecs) reads new ads and products so they start from what similar ones already learned. Each is explained at the bottom.
- Thirty ads that only change the backdrop still speak to one buyer with one reason, so Meta treats them as close to one ad. In the last six months of ads Galvor analysed, new ads that looked like many running ads got 36% less first-month spend.
- What you control now is the input: ads with a clear buyer, moment and reason to buy, and a product catalogue with rich titles and descriptions.

## Monday, 9:40 a.m.

Sam, our growth lead from [Issue #2](https://galvor.ai/newsletters/decode/false-bangers-why-your-best-hook-isnt-always-your-best-ad/), opens Ads Manager. A new column called Creative diversity says Low next to the ad set that pays the bills. Sam asks the agency for thirty new ads by Friday.

The agency takes the brief literally: new backdrops, new colours, a static, a carousel, an unboxing. Thirty ads that look nothing alike. Two weeks later, the old ad still takes the budget.

Every one of the thirty spoke to the same buyer, at the same moment, with the same reason to buy. They looked different. To Meta’s new process, they were similar.

> Thirty new looks. One buyer, one reason.

## Meta rebuilt three layers in October

![Diagram of Meta's three ad layers. Layer 1 Andromeda reads your ads: narrows tens of millions of ads to a shortlist for each person, over a billion ads scored a second. Layer 2 GEM reads the shopper: learns from the ads and posts each person engages with, about 19% more conversions since last year. Layer 3 GenRecs reads products and new ads: describes each ad by traits like brand, colour and style, shorter learning phase.](fig_01.jpg)

### 1 Andromeda reads your ads

- **What it is:** the shortlist. It picks the few thousand ads worth ranking for each person, out of tens of millions. Miss the shortlist and your ad never reaches the auction.
- **What Meta says:** it now scores every eligible ad, over a billion a second, 100 times the 2024 system, and has added 2.4% more conversions on Facebook since 2025.
- **What it means for you:** a new ad has a better chance of being considered early, but only if it looks and reads like a new ad.

### 2 GEM reads the shopper

- **What it is:** what Meta calls the “central brain” of its ad ranking. It learns from the ads and posts each person engages with, to predict what they will do next.
- **What Meta says:** it now reads twice as long a history per person, and has added about 19% more conversions since last year.
- **What it means for you:** you target through the creative. One shopper can care about time, proof and price at once, so Meta may show them several of your angles in a row.

### 3 GenRecs reads products and new ads

- **What it is:** a language model that describes every ad and product by traits such as brand, colour, fit and style, so a new ad starts from what similar ads already learned.
- **What Meta says:** it shortens the learning phase for new ads, though it doesn’t remove it.
- **What it means for you:** words count, not just pictures. Captions, scripts, on-screen text and your product catalogue (the titles and descriptions your store sends Meta) all tell it who you sell to.

## The one part you can see

The Creative diversity column started appearing in late August and reached most accounts in the last week of October. It labels each ad set high, medium or low:

>> “Creative diversity is calculated by comparing the images and video thumbnails in your ad set to each other to determine similarity.”
caption: Meta Ads Manager [help text](https://www.facebook.com/business/help/2371176336684086). Meta calls the metric estimated and in development.

![Two Ads Manager screenshots of the Creative diversity column: one rating four ad sets Low, one rating an ad set High.](fig_02.jpg)

The column only compares pictures. The three layers behind it read far more: your words, your buyer and your product. If the column rates an ad set Low, treat that as a smoke alarm, not a verdict.

## What Galvor saw in the data

Across the brands we work with, we keep seeing the same pattern. Here is how it looked in the last six months of ads Galvor analysed: every new video ad launched from May to September 2026, and how much of the budget it got in its first month.

![Galvor data, last six months. A new ad that looked like many running ads got 36% less first-month spend, in 4 of 5 months. Six or more look-alikes launched within three days each got 48% less. Against the average new ad: new look with a proven message +47%, familiar look with a proven message +15%, new look with a new message minus 1%, familiar look with a new message minus 16%.](fig_03.png)
caption: Source: Galvor analysis · ads launched May to Sep 2026

The bottom row is the one to remember. A new message over a familiar shot got 16% less: the script changed, but the ad still looked like one already running. A proven message in a new look did best, with 47% more. A new reason needs a new first shot.

## How to think about diversity: Galvor’s five layers

>> “Creative is the new targeting.”
>> “Your job is to give Meta enough creative diversity to match the right message to the right person at the right time.”
caption: Lines media buyers have repeated over two years of Andromeda

If the system reads ads, shoppers and products, a new ad has to be new in more than its look. Galvor scores every ad on five layers. Two are what the camera sees. Three are who the ad is for and what it says.

![Comparison chart. Look: same room, person and first shot with a new headline or colour is the same ad; a new setting, first shot or format is a new ad. Speaker: the same creator reading a new script is the same ad; an expert, a long-time customer or a first-timer is a new ad.](fig_04.jpg)

![Comparison chart. Audience: the same buyer in new words is the same ad; a new mom, a student or a gift buyer is a new ad. Stage: every ad pitching people who already know the brand is the same; ads for people who haven’t noticed the problem, are comparing options or are ready to buy are new. Reason: the same promise reworded is the same; texture, price or proof is new.](fig_05.jpg)

[box] The fix is usually smaller than you think

When we score a brand on these five layers, the fix list is short: a handful of new ads, each filling two or three gaps at once, and new opening seconds for a few ads that already sell. The recuts take hours of editing, not a new shoot.

**Galvor’s creative diversity score, out of 100, for a brand we work with:**

[stat] 63 | Before -> 92 | Two months after making the changes Galvor recommended

[/box]

## The shift for marketers and leaders

Five moves Galvor recommends.

### 1 Write for a reader, not only a viewer

Meta’s new ranking models and GenRecs read captions, scripts and on-screen text. Say who the product is for and what it fixes, in plain words. Fill in your product catalogue too: rich titles and descriptions help Meta match you today, and they are what shopping agents will read tomorrow.

### 2 Fund new buyers, not new versions

Meta’s own example of iteration is the same visuals with a new call to action, and it says iteration “should not replace true creative diversification”. In Galvor’s data, six or more look-alikes launched within three days each got 48% less first-month spend. Thirty edits of one shoot buy one ad.

### 3 Give new ads time, and treat a Low diversity rating as a smoke alarm

Galvor has seen some ad styles start about 35% dearer per order in their first two months and end close to average over their life. Judge new ads after weeks, not days, and use a test campaign to give ideas you believe in a fair share of spend. Meta’s Creative diversity column is still in development, and ad sets it rates Low have kept selling. Find out what is alike before you switch anything off.

### 4 Split every angle into motivation, situation and objection

A broad angle like “better sleep” is a family of ads, not one ad. Each motivation, situation and objection gives Meta a separate reason to match a different person.

![Diagram: the angle Better sleep splits into three motivations (stay sharp at work, wake up with energy, be more patient with my kids), three situations (mind racing after a stressful day, still awake before an early alarm, waking up at 3 a.m.) and three objections (will this work for me, I have tried others, how long before I notice), with an example ad frame for each. Brief each ad with five answers: who is it for, what situation, what reason to buy, what evidence, what will we learn.](fig_06.jpg)

### 5 Organise ad sets by buyer, not by angle

One shopper can care about saving time, proof and price at once, and Meta can now show them several angles in turn. One ad set per buyer, with each angle in the format that proves it best, gives it room to do that.

![Diagram: before, one ad set per angle (better sleep, energy, price), each holding versions. Now, one ad set per buyer (new parents; night-shift workers), each holding several angles matched to formats, such as proof as a testimonial video and price as a cost-per-use static.](fig_07.png)

## Explainer: The three systems, explained

**Andromeda.** Meta’s retrieval system. For every person and every ad slot, it narrows tens of millions of ads to a shortlist of a few thousand worth ranking. An ad that misses the shortlist never reaches the auction. [Meta’s post, 28 Oct 2026](https://engineering.fb.com/2026/10/28/ml-applications/meta-andromeda-next-gen-ads-retrieval-gpu-co-design/) {#andromeda}

**GEM.** Meta’s Generative Ads Model, which Meta calls the central brain of its ad ranking. It learns from what people do across Facebook and Instagram, in ads and in posts, and trains the models that rank ads. It doesn’t pick ads itself. [Meta’s post, 10 Nov 2025](https://engineering.fb.com/2025/11/10/ml-applications/metas-generative-ads-model-gem-the-central-brain-accelerating-ads-recommendation-ai-innovation/) {#gem}

**GenRecs.** Meta’s generative recommendations work. It uses language models to describe every ad and product with a shared set of building blocks, which Meta calls semantic tokens, so a brand-new ad can borrow what Meta has learned about similar ones. [Meta’s post, 19 Oct 2026](https://engineering.fb.com/2026/10/19/ml-applications/genrecs-tokenization-transforming-ads-recommendation-at-meta-with-stable-model-vocabulary/) {#genrecs}

## How we did this

Within ten days in October, Meta published two engineering posts ([19 Oct](https://engineering.fb.com/2026/10/19/ml-applications/genrecs-tokenization-transforming-ads-recommendation-at-meta-with-stable-model-vocabulary/), [28 Oct](https://engineering.fb.com/2026/10/28/ml-applications/meta-andromeda-next-gen-ads-retrieval-gpu-co-design/)) and briefed the trade press on a third change ([AdExchanger](https://www.adexchanger.com/ai/meta-has-a-new-ad-ranking-system-built-on-llms-plus-upgrades-to-andromeda-and-gem/)). The figures for each layer are Meta’s own.

Galvor’s data: new video ads launched from May to September 2026 by brands we work with, each followed for its first 30 days of spend and orders. We grouped ads by how they look and what they say, and compared each new ad’s first-month spend with the average new ad of its month. These are patterns, not experiments, and no brand is named. The cost-per-order point in move 3 looks at each ad’s whole life.

The five layers and the five moves are Galvor’s recommendations, drawn from our work with brands and from the sources below. Nobody outside Meta has measured the October changes yet.
